pages.observation: How I read it, left to right and top to bottom: (1) Panel 1, a full-width clinic waiting room. First the top-left caption 'Soon, his slot comes up.', then the top-right label 'NOW · A-12', which sits on the wall-mounted queue monitor. A smiling man in a green shirt with a shoulder bag stands by the blue seats, and a receptionist sits at a desk in the background. (2) Panel 2, bottom left. First the caption 'A quick vitals check first.', then the balloon 'Hi, Ravi! Just relax your arm for me.' Its short tail points down at the nurse in lilac scrubs, so I read her as the speaker, talking to the seated man (Ravi) while she takes his blood pressure. (3) Panel 3, bottom right. First the caption 'Dr. Ananya is notified when he's ready.', then the label 'RAVI · READY' on the tablet held by the doctor in a white coat. The order came naturally. There is only one balloon, so no reply is skipped. The balloon tail points at the right person. Neither the balloon nor the captions cover a face. The BP cuff, the bulb, the pulse oximeter and the doctor's face are all clear. Small issues: (a) The 'RAVI · READY' label covers most of the lower tablet screen and cuts through the check-mark icon above it. Its right end reaches the tablet edge, close to the doctor's right fingers, and its left end is near her left thumb. It does read as screen text, but it hides the on-screen check icon. Consider shrinking it or moving it up so the icon and her hands stay clear. (b) The 'NOW · A-12' box is drawn upright while the monitor is slightly angled. It still clearly belongs to that screen. (c) In panel 1 the man is not named; his name 'Ravi' first appears in the nurse's line in panel 2. This page alone does not show that A-12 is his number, so 'his slot' depends on earlier pages. (d) Panel 3 moves to a different room, the doctor's desk by a window. The caption explains the move well enough, but nothing shows whether this happens at the same time or later. The caption's present tense suggests the same time, and that is acceptable. None of these block reading. Only (a) is a real case of lettering covering on-screen detail and is worth fixing.
